lessons.text: Never mirror stem wording in answer options — rephrase distractors and correct answers to describe tactical outcomes, not the stem's details.
Only reference actors, positions, or prior events that were explicitly established in the stem — never introduce new assumed roles in answer options.
Phrase correct answer options in terms of outcomes or concepts, not echoes of stem wording — never restate the stem's key phrases in the correct choice.
Strip any stem-specific cues (directions, labels, identifiers) from answer options so test-takers must apply knowledge rather than pattern-match language.
Make all answer options roughly the same length — keep every option within 2–3 words of each other so length alone cannot signal the correct answer.
Avoid repeating key words or phrases from the question stem in any single answer option; rephrase so no option gets a lexical hint the others lack.
Force the stem to require an explicit read of the key concept variable — the player must diagnose *why* before choosing *what*, so instinct or position-sense alone cannot produce the correct answer.
Each distractor must have one clear, concept-tied flaw; eliminate options a strong player could reasonably defend on separate hockey logic.
Always verify that the `level` field matches a valid level for the target age group before writing the question.
Never hardcode a level string — look it up from the schema or constants to ensure it matches an accepted value.

Ensure every distractor is plausible but leads to an incorrect outcome — if a player correctly applies the concept being tested, no distractor should represent a reasonable next action they could defensibly take.
After drafting all options, argue for each distractor as correct; discard any you can successfully defend, then replace it with one whose logic breaks down under scrutiny.
